stories.body: Spain began three days of national mourning after a high-speed train travelling from Madrid to Seville collided with a stationary Iryo train near Urda, Toledo, killing at least 68 people and injuring many more. Emergency crews worked overnight to recover victims from wrecked carriages, some of which fell down an embankment, while authorities warned the death toll could rise. The government says the Iryo train had stopped after a computer failure and that a control centre subsequently allowed the Renfe train to resume at normal speed; investigators are examining why. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called the disaster unacceptable, particularly after another deadly high-speed crash on the same Madrid-Andalusia corridor earlier this year.
stories.headline: Spain begins three days of mourning after high-speed train crash kills at least 68

stories.body: Investigators are examining a 23-minute failure in the LZB rail-safety system and decisions taken at Adif's control centre before the Urda collision. Recordings reported by RTVE indicate that at 8:36am the Renfe driver was told to disconnect and reconnect the system and resume normal running, at speeds of up to 200 kilometres per hour, after the Urda control system failed. The Iryo driver later reported being stopped after losing transmission and said the train could not restart its LZB system. The government has described the crash as involving human error, while sources close to Iryo dispute aspects of that account. Separate judicial and technical investigations are expected to assess both the operational decisions and whether the older LZB system was adequate.
stories.headline: Investigators focus on control-centre decisions and signalling failure in Spain's deadly train collision

stories.body: The Toledo crash has suspended much of Spain's pre-election campaigning less than a month before the November 29 general election and put the government's stewardship of rail infrastructure under intense scrutiny. Sánchez has promised a full investigation and said safety measures would be strengthened if necessary, while Transport Minister Óscar Puente faces growing political pressure. Experts cited by El País argue that Spain has expanded its high-speed network faster than it has maintained existing tracks and systems: between 2018 and 2022, only 16% of high-speed spending went to maintenance, renewal and improvement. Opposition parties have demanded answers, while Vox continued campaigning and used the disaster to attack the government.
stories.headline: Train disaster reshapes Spain's pre-election campaign and intensifies scrutiny of rail safety

stories.body: On the second anniversary of the October 2024 floods in Valencia, which killed 233 people, reporting has renewed attention on delayed emergency alerts and the region's unfinished reconstruction. El País found that 182 people had died before the first mass ES-Alert was sent at 8:11pm, including José Fernández, who became trapped in an elevator after going to move his car as floodwaters rose. Residents and experts say zero risk is impossible in an area vulnerable to extreme rainfall and flash flooding, but they are calling for major flood-control works, safer development and better preparedness. Emergency repairs have been made, but larger projects to redirect waterways and protect communities remain pending.
stories.headline: Two years after the Valencia floods, families and experts press for accountability and stronger protection

stories.body: Canada and the European Union are expected to pursue an undefined "ever closer association" rather than launch talks on Canadian associate membership of the bloc. A draft statement for the EU-Canada summit in Montreal retreats from an idea floated by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, which had faced political and legal objections from member states. Prime Minister Mark Carney has sought closer European ties as Canada tries to reduce its reliance on the United States, but diplomats questioned what associate membership would mean for participation in EU institutions and decision-making.
stories.headline: Canada and EU drop associate-membership proposal while pursuing closer ties

stories.body: Military drone strikes in Nyala, the Rapid Support Forces' de facto capital in South Darfur, killed more than 100 people and wounded 113, according to the rights group Emergency Lawyers, although other casualty estimates are substantially lower and cannot be independently verified. Witnesses said the strike hit a busy market where RSF fighters had gathered alongside civilians, including women selling food and tea. Sudan Doctors Network initially reported 21 dead, while Médecins Sans Frontières said a hospital it supports received 36 bodies and treated more than 150 wounded after the market strike and a second strike on a civilian neighbourhood. The attack comes as Sudan's nearly four-year war increasingly relies on drones and continues to devastate civilian services.
stories.headline: Rights group says strikes on a Darfur market killed more than 100 people

stories.body: European natural-gas prices have risen above €100 per megawatt-hour for the first time since 2022 as winter nears. The EU says it is not concerned about immediate supply security, despite storage facilities being only 72% full, but has warned households that the coming season could be difficult. High energy costs are also prompting governments, including the United Kingdom's, to consider measures to cushion the effect on consumers.
stories.headline: European gas prices top €100 per megawatt-hour as winter approaches

stories.body: Vladimir Putin has hosted African leaders and government delegations in Moscow for the third Russia-Africa Summit, where talks are focused on trade, security, arms agreements and grain supplies. The Kremlin has presented African states as natural partners against the West, as it seeks to broaden Russia's political, military and economic footprint across the continent.
stories.headline: Putin hosts African leaders in Moscow as Russia seeks to expand its influence across the continent

stories.body: An Egyptian court has ordered the independent outlet Mada Masr closed and fined its editor-in-chief, Lina Attalah, 3 million Egyptian pounds after convicting her of managing an unlicensed website. Attalah was briefly detained and released after the fine was paid; her lawyer said she had also been sentenced in absentia in 2024 to a year in prison, a ruling under appeal. Rights groups say the action, alongside the recent detention of staff at the fact-checking outlet Matsadaash, signals an escalating campaign to eliminate Egypt's remaining independent media.
stories.headline: Egypt shuts independent outlet Mada Masr and fines its editor in new press-freedom crackdown

stories.body: The Federal Reserve held its benchmark interest-rate range at 3.75% to 4%, pausing after its first increase in more than three years in September. The 10-2 decision came less than a week before the November 3 midterm elections, with governors Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack voting for another quarter-point increase. Chair Kevin Warsh said the Fed needs more information before deciding on its next move, acknowledging that inflation remains too high while arguing that tightening financial conditions indicate the previous increase is beginning to work. The next policy meeting is scheduled for December 8-9.
stories.headline: Federal Reserve holds interest rates steady days before US midterm elections

stories.body: Voters in 39 states will decide 145 statewide ballot measures this November, with at least $400 million already spent on television advertising. California's Proposition 40, the costliest contest, would impose a one-time 5% tax on billionaires, while a separate proposition could nullify it if both pass. Other measures concern redistricting, abortion access, voting rules and transgender rights; five states have initiatives involving transgender issues, the largest such set of ballot questions to date. Four states will consider abortion-access measures, while more than a dozen will vote on election-administration rules, including voter-ID and citizenship requirements.
stories.headline: Voters in 39 states face consequential ballot measures on wealth taxes, abortion, voting and transgender rights

stories.body: Utah has filed criminal charges against prediction-market platform Kalshi and its co-founders, Tarek Mansour and Luana Lopes Lara, alleging that the company illegally promoted online gambling. The complaint says Kalshi accepted bets by an undercover officer on sporting events and includes 12 counts of online gambling promotion, a general gambling-promotion count and a pattern-of-unlawful-activity count. The case escalates a broader dispute between states and the Trump administration over whether prediction markets fall under federal commodities regulation or state gambling laws, after a judge ruled in August that Utah could enforce its anti-gambling law against such platforms.
stories.headline: Prediction-market company Kalshi and its co-founders face criminal charges in Utah

stories.body: Spain's railway drivers' union, Semaf, is maintaining a nationwide strike at Renfe after the fatal high-speed crash in Toledo, saying it wants structural improvements to rail safety and is considering further action. The stoppage affects all Renfe train-driving staff and is expected to cause major disruption, including to Rodalies and regional services in Catalonia, which will operate under minimum-service rules. Semaf says its demands include enforceable protocols for severe-weather alerts, clearer risk communications, proper rest arrangements and a workplace culture in which drivers can report safety problems without fear of punishment.
stories.headline: Renfe drivers proceed with safety strike in wake of Toledo rail disaster

stories.body: Mossos d'Esquadra are investigating the violent death of a woman in Barcelona's Nou Barris district after a man surrendered to police in Madrid and reportedly confessed to killing his former partner. Officers and firefighters found the woman's body after receiving a report that she was not responding inside a home. The case is under judicial secrecy and has been assigned to a Barcelona court specialising in violence against women. If confirmed as a gender-based killing, it would be the fifth such death in Catalonia this year.
stories.headline: Police investigate killing of woman in Barcelona's Nou Barris district after man surrenders in Madrid

stories.body: Catalan police are preparing for possible renewed disorder in Barcelona this Saturday after calls on social media to repeat last weekend's violence and looting. Authorities say accounts on TikTok and Telegram have been removed, but at least one active call worries police because it has a channel actively promoting it and messages have openly discussed robbery and assaults on officers. A total of 133 people have now been detained over the October 24 unrest, including 85 minors. Mossos leaders described the episode as an unprecedented form of youth violence in Catalonia, marked by its scale, violence and rapid online mobilisation.
stories.headline: Catalan police prepare for possible renewed unrest after youth violence and looting in Barcelona

stories.body: The Port of Barcelona has approved a €104.5 million project to replace its Terminal C cruise facility and later demolish terminals A and B, reducing the number of cruise terminals from seven to five. Terminal C is due to close after its final operation this weekend, after which it will be emptied and demolished for construction of a new 11,253-square-metre terminal with solar generation and shore-power connections for ships. The new terminal will prioritise home-port and smaller premium vessels, while the later removal of terminals A and B will enable a broader renovation of the Moll Adossat. The port says the changes will reduce cruise capacity by 16%.
stories.headline: Barcelona Port commits €104.5 million to new cruise terminal while removing two existing terminals
